title: What to Know About the U.S. Army's Controversial Lead Detonation in Iowa
author: Chad de Guzman; Connor Greene
body:
The U.S. Army carried out its contentious plan to blow up more than five dozen barrels of a toxic explosive chemical in an Iowa munitions plant on Wednesday, despite pushback from environmental activists and local politicians.

A controlled explosion of nearly five tons of degraded lead azide, a chemical compound used as a detonator in cartridges and shells, took place at around 9 a.m. local time (10 a.m. ET) at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a city of nearly 400 people in Des Moines County, some 13 km away from the Mississippi River separating the state from Illinois.

The Army has argued that a controlled, on-site blast was the safest way to dispose of the lead azide stockpiles, which became unstable after prolonged storage and were at increased risk of exploding on their own due to falling temperatures.

“The choice that we faced here was between a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation of dangerous material or a controlled detonation where we could choose the time, and place to optimize the conditions and deliver the best result not just for our operations, but for the safety of the public and the surrounding communities,” Assistant Secretary of the Army Jordan Gillis said in a video statement on Wednesday.

By Wednesday evening, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said that its real-time air monitors reported “ZERO” detection of airborne lead, which it said “has remained consistent before, during, and after this morning’s controlled detonation.” The agency added that 300 of its personnel were sampling air, land, and water “across the region,” to compare with over 1,200 samples it collected before the detonation.

“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” Major General Eric P. Shirley said during a press conference providing an update about two hours after the explosion, calling the operation “tremendously successful” and confirming that there was “no infrastructure damage in or around our installation.”

As ongoing air monitoring results showed no detectable lead, the Federal Emergency Management Agency said Wednesday afternoon that an earlier shelter-in-place order has been lifted.

President Donald Trump lauded the detonation as a “great job by the Army,” on his Truth Social account. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin similarly told CNN that the operation “exceeded expectations.”

The EPA previously announced that it has been on the ground since before the explosion and would “be here for as long as necessary AFTER detonation to ensure communities are safe.”

Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy Jr. added on Wednesday that per Trump’s directions, Health and Human Services (HHS) had “deployed personnel to Iowa to help protect families and support local officials throughout this operation,” and that officials from the department would “stay on the ground to support the community through the response and recovery.”

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also said it had activated an emergency response to support HHS to “provide accurate public health communication and technical assistance to our state and federal partners.”

Here’s what to know about the situation and how it got to this point.

How did we get here?

According to a Nov. 20 letter from a regional administrator of the EPA to Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds, the EPA was first notified in March of 68 drums of potentially unstable lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.

The Army said in October that it had discovered the stockpile during “a routine stockpile surveillance operation at the plant.”

Between April and September, the EPA issued three emergency storage permits so the Army could continue storing the stockpile safely while the Army assessed how to treat it.

In October, the Army said it determined the “safest course of action is to neutralize the material on-site via an intentional, controlled detonation,” and it held a public meeting for the community.

On Nov. 13, the regional EPA granted an emergency permit to detonate the stockpiles between then and Feb. 11, 2027. Two days later, the Army announced it planned for a Nov. 20 detonation.

Since then, the detonation schedule has been repeatedly put off amid pushback from environmental activists and politicians concerned about potential health hazards.

Lead is a neurotoxin health officials have long documented to cause a variety of health problems in pregnant women and children. There is no safe exposure level to lead: exposed children can suffer damage to the brain and nervous system, learning and behavioral issues, speech and hearing impairments, while pregnant women face increased risks of premature births and miscarriages.

The Army argued it could not afford delays, however, as its window to safely dispose of the stockpiles was shrinking with winter’s arrival. Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist for the Army Sustainment Command, told a local news station on Nov. 18 that colder temperatures could cause the lead azide to detonate spontaneously.

“This is not something that we take lightly,” Barati said. “We know that this is a disruption to people and that is not our intent, but we’re trying to do this in the safest manner possible.”

On Nov. 19, environmental groups sued the EPA over its permit for the detonation. The same day, a bipartisan group of Illinois politicians—Democratic U.S. Senators Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth of Illinois; Democratic Lieutenant Governor and U.S. Senator-elect Juliana Stratton, Democratic U.S. Representative Eric Sorensen; Democratic Governor JB Pritzker; and Republican U.S. Representatives Darin LaHood and Mary Miller—as well as the U.S. Senator-elect for Iowa Josh Turek, sent a letter expressing concerns about the detonation and urging Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to consider delaying it.

Later on Nov. 19, Telle announced the explosion would be postponed from Nov. 20 to Nov. 23, and a federal appeals court ordered a temporary freeze on the detonations permit.

Then, on Nov. 21, the Justice Department said it planned to use emergency powers to avoid the permit requirement for detonation. The department emphasized the “immediate risk” posed by the stockpile, while saying that the Army “intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect.”

On Nov. 22, the Army rescheduled the blast for Nov. 25, saying that the new schedule would “allow for more optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.”

Trump weighed in on Nov. 23, saying in a social media post that he had ordered the military to postpone the planned detonation until the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit cleared the way and only if Iowa’s Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand agreed to the operation.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump said.

Later that day, the court lifted a temporary stay on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency permit for the detonation. It deemed that the agency incorporated adequate safeguards to minimize the dispersal of potentially hazardous dust and mitigate risks.

Sand had criticized the Army’s previously stated plans to go ahead with the detonation of the stockpiles despite the court-issued pause, after the Department of Justice said it would use emergency powers to avoid the requirement for an EPA permit.

“Because of the decisions that have already been made over the course of months, if not years, no good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been,” Sand posted on Nov. 22.

On Nov. 23, he deferred to the Trump Administration and experts to decide, posting: “The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks.” He again appealed for more transparency, adding: “Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward.”

After the appeals court gave the go ahead, the Army pushed through with its plan to detonate the lead azide on Nov. 25.

What are environmentalists’ and politicians’ concerns?

Environmental groups have argued that the U.S. Army is “sidestepping” the judicial process. They claim that the EPA approved the detonation plan without enough public notice and without thoroughly studying alternatives.

Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club, both nonprofit environmental advocacy organizations, argued in their suit filed before the appellate court that the permit authorized the Army to detonate the lead azide “in the open,” adding that the blast would create “a plume of lead dust that will blanket homes and communities” possibly as far as 100 mi or more. The petitioners emphasized that there’s no safe level of exposure to lead.

They also argued that the Army did not promptly and accurately inform the public of the detonation and its impact, claiming that many residents and local officials only learned of the planned detonation “through friends and social media.”

In the Army’s public notice issued just days before the initial blast schedule, it said the lead azide barrels will be detonated in two, rapid-fire shots inside concrete, earth-covered magazines surrounded by Hesco barriers filled with sand about two stories high. Before and during the detonation, the soil above the magazines will be saturated with water, and water misters will be spraying, all in an attempt to control the amount of lead that could travel through the air beyond the plant.

The notice added that models projected the level of lead particles in the air after the detonation “may be elevated but well below the level at which EPA would require protective actions be taken.” Middletown residents can expect the plume to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed, the notice said.

The Army said safety measures will be in place but advised residents to evacuate and avoid the affected area in Iowa and urged those who could not leave to stay indoors, close windows and doors, and turn off heating and cooling systems that could bring in outside air. It also said residents should wet-clean surfaces to remove lead dust.

The potential health risk caused by the detonation threatens Iowa, which is already suffering from having one of the highest cancer incidences in the U.S., as well as neighboring Illinois. Both states have since taken measures ahead of the planned detonations: Iowa’s state Homeland Security and Emergency Management department launched a dedicated website containing updates and guidance for residents, while Illinois’ state Environmental Protection Agency launched a similar dashboard.

Illinois’ EPA said the detonation is expected to produce a “dust plume containing lead particles” that could travel beyond the plant and deposit on surrounding surfaces. Agriculture officials in the state recommended ways to protect livestock and pets, including keeping animals indoors until the plume passes.

“The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point,” said Wally Taylor, attorney for the environmental organization Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter, one of the petitioners against the EPA. “However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources.”
